transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Medina (Rivermark), Anya Patel (Rivermark), Ravi Shah (Rivermark Sec)

Summary: quick check-in on latency numbers from last week's run, confirm TTFT, streaming issues, and next tuning steps.

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, is this a good time?
00:08 Carlos: yeah morning - afternoon - sorry, afternoon Jordan. All good here.
00:12 Priya: hey, quick note, I've uploaded the perf traces from the dedicated cluster run, see the links in the deck. Some of the kernel selector logs were noisy but should be helpful.
00:25 Anya: cool, saw that, trying to pull them now. We saw a regression in TTFT when streaming was turned on last week, so that's one of the main items.
00:37 Jordan: yep that's what we're here for - to walk through root cause and next steps. Priya, can you start with the top-level TL;DR from the traces?
00:45 Priya: sure. TL;DR: overall token latency is fine at steady state, but TTFT spikes when we enable streaming at shorter sequences. The kernel selector sometimes picks a fallback kernel when the sequence length distribution shifts, which adds a 30-70ms hit in some cases. Also noticed KV cache warmup cost on cold prefixes.
01:10 Carlos: by "fallback kernel" do you mean the old cu-attn path, or something else? Our SE flagged "kernel selector" picking a non-optimized path.
01:20 Priya: yea that's right, sometimes the runtime chooses the generic kernel when the batched sequence shapes don't match the optimized kernel heuristics. We saw it on the 2x A100 equivalent nodes during bursts.
01:35 Ravi: just to flag security side, any change to runtime or model variants will need to go through our audit trail since we have to validate KMS usage and image signing.
01:45 Jordan: good call, Ravi. We'll include the exact commit and selector logs when we share artifacts. Priya, do we have approximate numbers for TTFT delta with streaming on?
01:55 Priya: ballpark from the traces: TTFT goes from ~78ms steady to 140-220ms in the worst streaming cases we replayed. But that's with a misaligned batch and fallback kernel. When the proper kernel is used, TTFT is 65-85ms.
02:20 Anya: interesting. Our baseline in-house tests were targeting ~90ms TTFT at 256 seq; the 220ms is concerning. Are there config knobs for the selector?
02:30 Priya: yes, there's a couple: 1) adjust kernel selection thresholds to prefer quantized kernels for our seq distribution; 2) tweak continuous batching window to avoid very small micro-batches when streaming; 3) enable prefix KV caching more aggressively to avoid cold-path cost. We'll share exact flags.
02:50 Carlos: when you say "quantized kernels" do we lose quality? Our legal team is sensitive to any output drift.
02:58 Priya: good question. For the 4-bit quant profiles we tested, delta in output was negligible on our eval set. But we should run your curated prompts against the quantized variant. Also, we can selectively quantize (last layers) to minimize shift.
03:20 Jordan: note for later - run customer evals on quantized variant and add to quality monitoring rapid suite.
03:27 Carlos: agreed.
03:30 Priya: another point: streaming implementation in your client was chunking at 64 tokens which increases overhead per chunk. If you increase chunk sizes to 128 or do adaptive chunking, TTFT improves because we amortize the dispatch overhead. But that does affect perceived latency for first few tokens depending on how you stream.
03:55 Anya: hmm, we did 64 to be conservative. We can try 128 but worried about UX - some of our product flows expect earlier partial output.
04:05 Jordan: tradeoff -- earlier partial output vs overall TTFT. We can run A/B to see user impact. Priya, can you recommend an adaptive threshold?
04:15 Priya: start with 96-128 for seqs around 256; for seqs 512+, go to 128-192. We'll capture perf vs perceived latency metrics.
04:28 Carlos: can you explain the KV cache warmup you mentioned? We did see periodic bumps that aligned with new prefixes in our traffic.
04:35 Priya: sure. If the request uses novel prefixes, the runtime warms KV entries which causes a one-off cost when cache miss occurs. On our side we have an aggressive prefix caching strategy but your workload had many unique prefixes because of long transaction IDs. Two mitigations: prefix normalization (strip or hash stable parts) and sticky routing to keep hot keys on same workers.
05:05 Ravi: sticky routing has implications with failover. If we keep sticky to reduce cache misses, do we compromise reliability?
05:12 Priya: we can do best-effort sticky with fallback policies. If a node is down the router falls back to pooled routing. It should be transparent but we'll show metrics on failover experiments.
05:22 Anya: can we also see how quantization + sticky routing combos behave? Might be additive for latency but need to ensure not regressing quality.
05:30 Priya: yes, we'll create a small matrix test: quantized vs FP16 and sticky vs pooled and measure TTFT and token latency.
05:39 Jordan: good. Now about kernel selector - is there a quick config change we can flip to avoid that fallback you observed?
05:46 Priya: yes, on the runtime you can raise the "preferred kernel sharpness" flag which biases selection towards optimized kernel if memory headroom exists. That cuts the fallback occurrences by ~70% in our internal runs. Downside: slight memory overhead; for your Dedicated pool we have headroom but we need to confirm with your instance sizes.
06:12 Carlos: what numbers on memory overhead? We have tight packing to meet throughput requirements.
06:18 Priya: add roughly 8-12% GPU memory per model instance depending on quant profile; exact numbers in the logs I'll share. If memory is constrained we can instead tune batching window which is lower risk.
06:30 Anya: batching window - are you referring to continuous batching? We saw some queueing when bursts hit.
06:35 Priya: yes. Continuous batching window is how long the runtime waits to aggregate small inputs into a batch. Longer window yields better throughput but worse latency; shorter window reduces batching benefits and increases kernel selector churn. There's a sweet spot for your workload because you have many short prompts.
06:55 Carlos: our traffic is bursty around reconciliation windows, short prompts with variable seq lengths. So maybe adaptive window makes sense.
07:03 Priya: exact. We recommend adaptive windows: smaller during low qps, aggressive batching during high qps. Our autoscaler + sampler can flip windows based on queue slope.
07:18 Ravi: does that interact with our cost projections? If you batch more aggressively during high qps, will we see fewer tokens billed or just lower per-token latency?
07:28 Jordan: batching reduces per-token compute overhead so cost-per-token drops a bit, but billing granularity remains tokens. You'll see lower engineering cost due to fewer concurrent instances required for throughput. We'll provide a cost sensitivity chart.
07:45 Anya: ok. Back to streaming: you mentioned the client chunk size and adaptive approach. If we change to 128, does the server need config?
07:52 Priya: no server changes required, it's client-side. But we can also enable a server-side smoothing hook that tries to fill small chunks from cache to avoid micro-dispatches; that is a runtime flag we can flip in Dedicated. For hosted it's gated by our config and we'd need to push for it.
08:10 Carlos: is that the same as the "stream smoothing" we tried briefly? We thought it added latency in some cases.
08:16 Priya: probably different. The smoothing I mean coalesces very small chunks into one dispatch if it expects more tokens imminently; that reduces TTFT overhead. The previous setting may have been delaying first token to fill buffer which hurts perceived latency; we'll tune it to not delay first token.
08:36 Jordan: great. Next, sequence length tradeoffs - you tested 256 vs 512 in runs?
08:43 Priya: yes. For 512 we saw overall per-token latency slightly higher because of longer KV handling and different kernel choices. TTFT also increased slightly. But throughput per GPU improved for long sequences. If your workload mainly uses 256, we should optimize for that.
09:02 Carlos: most of our interactive flows are 256 or less, but reconciliation jobs hit 512+ sometimes. We care more about interactive tails.
09:12 Priya: then we recommend pinning canary routes to 256-optimized kernels and use a separate pool for background batch jobs at 512. Redwood Dedicated supports multi-pool routing - can do that.
09:26 Anya: what's the easiest way to split routes? We use tags in our API currently.
09:30 Jordan: just assign model routes with metadata tag route=interactive vs route=batch; our router policy can route based on that header. We'll share a snippet.
09:40 Carlos: perfect. Now, are there any quick wins we can do this week to reduce TTFT?
09:46 Priya: quick wins: 1) bump streaming chunk to 96-128 on client; 2) flip kernel selector sharpness flag in canary; 3) enable more aggressive KV prefix caching for hot keys; 4) run one synthetic TTFT pass with sticky routing enabled. Those should be doable in a week.
10:06 Jordan: sounds good. We'll prioritize the kernel selector change in canary and share the exact flag. Priya, will you include commands?
10:12 Priya: yes, will paste the runtime flags and the perf traces to the shared folder. Expect them by Friday (2027-12-16).
10:20 Carlos: on the security side, we need the exact commit hashes for the runtime change to run our image-signing checks. Ravi, can you coordinate?
10:27 Ravi: yep I'll need the artifact and the SBOM. Also need to know if KMS use changes for any key wrapping.
10:33 Priya: KMS usage doesn't change for these tuning flags; it's purely runtime config. We'll include SBOM and the runtime build ID.
10:40 Anya: one more question - quantization. We want to run a quick quality regression on our top-100 prompts. Can you provide a script to run locally?
10:48 Priya: yes, we'll provide a test harness that hits the quantized model and collects outputs in the format you need. We'll include diff metrics and suggest thresholds.
10:58 Jordan: perfect. Anything else from the Rivermark side?
11:02 Carlos: just to confirm, we'll run TTFT at seq=512 with streaming enabled and include client chunk size 64 and 128 to compare. We'll attach logs and traces.
11:12 Priya: great, that'll give us good matrix. If you can also include a sample of the long prefixes causing KV misses that helps.
11:18 Anya: will do.
11:20 Jordan: ok quick recap and next steps: Priya shares kernel logs + flags by 12/16; Carlos runs TTFT matrix by 12/18; Jordan sends pricing by 12/20; schedule streaming deep-dive for 12/21. Any objections?
11:36 Carlos: none.
11:37 Ravi: no.
11:38 Priya: all good. I'll tag the artifacts in the shared folder.
11:43 Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in Slack with links. End call.

Notes: occasional transcription errors - product names sometimes appear as "Reedwood" or "Redwood Devoted" in auto transcript. Speaker attributions approximate. References to logs and decks are in shared folder link: https://redwood.example.com/share/rivermark/latency-weekly-20271214
